subtopic_detail: Proximal weakness and bone pain with an alkaline phosphatase of 340 and a bone density T score of minus 2.8 in a housebound woman
stem:
You are the physician seeing a 64 year old woman referred after a bone density scan requested by her general practitioner returned a lumbar spine T score of minus 2.8. The referral asks you to start treatment for osteoporosis.

She has been largely housebound for three years since a stroke left her with a mild left hemiparesis, and she goes outside only for appointments. She describes aching in her hips and thighs and says she now has to push up on the arms of the chair to stand. Her gait is waddling when she walks with her stick. She takes no calcium or vitamin D supplement and eats little dairy.

data_table.Examination: Mild residual left hemiparesis, proximal weakness of hip flexion and shoulder abduction graded 4 out of 5 bilaterally, waddling gait, tenderness on firm pressure over both anterior tibiae and the sternum, no joint swelling
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.08 mmol/L (2.20 to 2.60), phosphate 0.71 mmol/L (0.75 to 1.50), alkaline phosphatase 340 U/L (30 to 110), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 11 nmol/L (greater than 50), parathyroid hormone markedly elevated, creatinine 74 micromol/L with an estimated glomerular filtration rate greater than 60 mL/min/1.73m2, liver function tests otherwise within normal limits, bone density lumbar spine T score minus 2.8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Start alendronate weekly and review her bone density in two years
options.rationale: Starting an antiresorptive agent in a patient with profound vitamin D deficiency and a calcium at the lower limit risks precipitating symptomatic hypocalcaemia, and the low bone density here reflects defective mineralisation rather than the bone loss that bisphosphonates treat. Vitamin D status must be corrected before any antiresorptive is considered. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management algorithm)
source_refs: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management algorithm

options.text: Start denosumab six monthly and review her bone density in two years
options.rationale: Denosumab carries the same hypocalcaemia hazard as other antiresorptive agents and a greater one, since its effect cannot be withdrawn once the injection is given. Correcting vitamin D and calcium before starting it is a specific requirement of its use. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management algorithm)
source_refs: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management algorithm

options.text: Replace vitamin D and calcium, then reassess before any antiresorptive
options.rationale: Proximal myopathy, bone pain, a low calcium and phosphate, a markedly raised alkaline phosphatase and a 25 hydroxyvitamin D of 11 nmol/L describe osteomalacia, in which the bone is undermineralised rather than reduced in quantity, and repletion alone improves symptoms, biochemistry and measured bone density. Reassessment after repletion determines whether any residual bone density deficit warrants specific osteoporosis treatment. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management algorithm)
source_refs: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management algorithm

options.text: Start teriparatide daily and review her bone density in eighteen months
options.rationale: An anabolic agent is reserved for severe osteoporosis with fractures despite antiresorptive therapy and is not a treatment for undermineralised bone. Its use in untreated vitamin D deficiency would also risk hypercalcaemia once repletion occurred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start calcitriol daily and review her bone density in eighteen months
options.rationale: Calcitriol bypasses hepatic and renal hydroxylation and is reserved for renal disease or hydroxylase deficiency, neither of which applies with a normal estimated glomerular filtration rate. The near pair here is that the parent compound at repletion doses is what corrects a nutritional deficiency, with a much wider safety margin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Osteomalacia and osteoporosis both reduce measured bone density but are entirely different diseases, the first a failure to mineralise osteoid and the second a loss of otherwise normal bone, and treating one as the other is a recognised clinical error. The clues to defective mineralisation are proximal myopathy with a waddling gait, bone pain and tenderness rather than the painlessness of uncomplicated osteoporosis, and a biochemical pattern of low or low normal calcium and phosphate with a raised alkaline phosphatase and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Risk is concentrated in people with little sun exposure, including housebound and residential care populations, those who cover their skin, and those with malabsorption, and Australian practice is to measure 25 hydroxyvitamin D in these groups rather than universally. Repletion produces marked symptomatic improvement over weeks to months and raises bone density substantially, so the decision about antiresorptive therapy is deferred until the deficiency is corrected and the scan repeated.
key_points: Proximal myopathy and bone tenderness point to defective mineralisation
Low calcium and phosphate with a raised alkaline phosphatase is the biochemical signature
Antiresorptive therapy in untreated deficiency risks symptomatic hypocalcaemia
Repletion itself raises measured bone density substantially
Normal renal function makes the parent compound appropriate rather than calcitriol
explanation.pearls: Alkaline phosphatase rises further in the first weeks after vitamin D repletion begins, as the accumulated osteoid mineralises, so a higher value at the six week review indicates healing rather than treatment failure and should not prompt a change of plan.

sources.label: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management algorithm

subtopic_detail: Deranged liver enzymes with a new tremor and deteriorating handwriting in a twenty four year old whose caeruloplasmin is low
stem:
You are the physician seeing a 24 year old man referred with four months of abnormal liver enzymes found when he was investigated for tiredness. He drinks about four standard drinks a week and takes no regular medication, supplements or protein powders.

His girlfriend has persuaded him to come because his handwriting has become small and untidy over the same period and he has started dropping things. He has also become withdrawn and irritable and has dropped out of his university course. On examination there is a coarse tremor of both outstretched arms that worsens when he holds them flexed in front of his chest, and his speech is slightly slurred. His caeruloplasmin is 0.08 g/L.

data_table.Examination: Coarse proximal tremor of both arms worse on sustained posture, mild dysarthria, no asterixis, no jaundice, liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin, spleen not palpable, no ascites, gait normal
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 168 U/L (less than 45), aspartate aminotransferase 194 U/L (less than 40), alkaline phosphatase 42 U/L (30 to 110), bilirubin 28 micromol/L (less than 20), international normalised ratio 1.2 (0.9 to 1.3), caeruloplasmin 0.08 g/L (0.20 to 0.60), haemoglobin 108 g/L (130 to 180) with a negative direct antiglobulin test, hepatitis B and C serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Measure serum alpha 1 antitrypsin and review when the result returns
options.rationale: Alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency causes liver disease in young adults but has no neurological or psychiatric manifestations and does not cause a Coombs negative haemolysis. It does not explain the combination in front of you. (Source: GESA: Wilson disease clinical update)

options.text: Measure serum ferritin and transferrin saturation, then review the result
options.rationale: Iron overload presents in middle age with arthropathy, diabetes and skin pigmentation rather than in the twenties with tremor and psychiatric change. The near pair here is that both are inherited metabolic liver diseases, but the age and the neurological features separate them clearly. (Source: GESA: Wilson disease clinical update)

options.text: Arrange liver biopsy for histology before any other investigation
options.rationale: Hepatic copper quantification on biopsy is a useful confirmatory test but is invasive and is reserved for cases that remain uncertain after non invasive testing. Performing it first exposes him to a procedure that the urine and eye examination may make unnecessary. (Source: GESA: Wilson disease clinical update)

options.text: Measure 24 hour urinary copper and arrange slit lamp examination
options.rationale: A low caeruloplasmin is suggestive but insufficient on its own, since it falls in any severe liver disease and in protein loss and is normal in up to a tenth of affected patients, so the diagnosis is built from a raised 24 hour urinary copper excretion together with corneal copper deposition seen on slit lamp examination. Rings are present in almost all patients who have neurological involvement, which makes the eye examination particularly informative in this presentation. (Source: GESA: Wilson disease clinical update)

options.text: Measure autoantibodies and immunoglobulins, then review the result
options.rationale: Autoimmune hepatitis is a reasonable consideration in a young person with hepatitis and is worth testing, but it does not produce a low caeruloplasmin, a movement disorder or a Coombs negative haemolytic anaemia. Pursuing it first would delay the diagnosis that explains every finding. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Wilson disease)

explanation.summary: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive defect of biliary copper excretion that presents between childhood and the fourth decade, with hepatic disease dominating in younger patients and neuropsychiatric disease in older ones, and the two frequently overlap. The neurological picture is a movement disorder, classically a coarse wing beating tremor, dysarthria, dystonia and parkinsonism, and psychiatric presentations with personality change, irritability and academic decline are common and often precede diagnosis by years. Coombs negative haemolytic anaemia occurs when copper is released from dying hepatocytes, and the combination of haemolysis with liver disease in a young person is a particularly strong pointer. No single test is sufficient, so diagnosis combines a low caeruloplasmin, a raised basal 24 hour urinary copper excretion, corneal deposition on slit lamp examination and, where doubt remains, hepatic copper quantification or genetic testing.
key_points: Hepatic and neuropsychiatric features frequently coexist in the same patient
Caeruloplasmin is neither sensitive nor specific enough to diagnose alone
Corneal rings are present in nearly all patients with neurological involvement
Coombs negative haemolysis with liver disease in a young person is a strong pointer
A low alkaline phosphatase relative to the bilirubin is characteristic in acute presentations
explanation.pearls: First degree relatives of a newly diagnosed patient must be screened even when completely asymptomatic, because treatment started before organ damage occurs prevents the disease entirely, whereas a sibling identified after cirrhosis has developed has already lost that opportunity.

subtopic_detail: Increased left ventricular wall thickness with low voltage electrocardiogram complexes and nephrotic range proteinuria in a sixty seven year old
stem:
You are the physician seeing a 67 year old man with six months of breathlessness on exertion, ankle swelling that now reaches his thighs, and light headedness when he stands. He has never been hypertensive and his blood pressure readings in your clinic have been in the low normal range.

He has noticed that his urine froths in the toilet bowl. He also mentions that he has bitten the side of his tongue several times recently and that bruises appear around his eyes when he coughs hard. His jugular venous pressure is elevated at 7 cm and there is pitting oedema to the thighs. The echocardiogram reports a left ventricular wall thickness of 16 mm with a granular sparkling myocardial texture and impaired longitudinal strain, while the electrocardiogram shows low voltage complexes in all limb leads.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/66 mmHg lying and 86/58 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Jugular venous pressure elevated at 7 cm, pitting oedema to the thighs, enlarged tongue with lateral indentations, periorbital purpura, liver edge palpable 3 cm below the costal margin, chest clear on auscultation
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein to creatinine ratio 620 mg/mmol (less than 30), serum albumin 24 g/L (35 to 50), creatinine 132 micromol/L (60 to 110), N terminal pro B type natriuretic peptide markedly elevated, high sensitivity troponin mildly and persistently elevated without a rise and fall, electrocardiogram shows low voltage complexes in all limb leads, echocardiogram reports a left ventricular wall thickness of 16 mm with granular myocardial texture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Measure serum free light chains with serum and urine immunofixation
options.rationale: Thickened ventricular walls with low voltage complexes is a discordance that excludes hypertrophy and indicates infiltration, and the combination with nephrotic range proteinuria, an enlarged tongue and periorbital purpura points to light chain deposition. Free light chains with immunofixation detect the clonal protein in over 98 per cent of cases and identify the plasma cell disorder that treatment is actually directed against. (Source: HSANZ: Systemic amyloidosis diagnosis and management)
source_refs: HSANZ: Systemic amyloidosis diagnosis and management

options.text: Arrange coronary angiography and review once it has been reported
options.rationale: The persistently elevated troponin without a rise and fall reflects ongoing myocardial injury from infiltration rather than an acute coronary syndrome, and there is no chest pain or dynamic change. Angiography would not explain the proteinuria, the tongue or the purpura. (Source: HSANZ: Systemic amyloidosis diagnosis and management)
source_refs: HSANZ: Systemic amyloidosis diagnosis and management

options.text: Start an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor and review in six weeks
options.rationale: Standard heart failure therapy is poorly tolerated in infiltrative disease because the stiff ventricle depends on preload and the patient already has a significant postural drop. Treating empirically before the diagnosis is made risks profound hypotension. (Source: HSANZ: Systemic amyloidosis diagnosis and management)
source_refs: HSANZ: Systemic amyloidosis diagnosis and management

options.text: Arrange cardiac magnetic resonance imaging before any blood testing
options.rationale: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is valuable for characterising infiltration but it cannot identify the protein responsible, and the distinction between light chain and transthyretin deposition determines entirely different treatment. Blood testing for a clonal protein is quicker, cheaper and more decisive. (Source: HSANZ: Systemic amyloidosis diagnosis and management)
source_refs: HSANZ: Systemic amyloidosis diagnosis and management

options.text: Refer for renal biopsy before any other investigation is arranged
options.rationale: Tissue diagnosis is necessary but is usually obtained first from a low risk site such as abdominal fat aspirate or bone marrow rather than from an organ, particularly where bleeding risk is increased. The near pair here is that a renal biopsy becomes appropriate if the screening tests and the less invasive tissue sampling are unrevealing. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Amyloidosis)

explanation.summary: Increased ventricular wall thickness with low voltage complexes on the electrocardiogram is a discordance that should never be attributed to hypertrophy, because true hypertrophy increases voltage, and it is the single most useful pointer to an infiltrative cardiomyopathy. Light chain amyloidosis arises from a clonal plasma cell population producing misfolded immunoglobulin light chains that deposit in the heart, kidneys, liver, nerves and soft tissues, and the classic soft tissue signs of macroglossia and periorbital purpura are highly specific though present in only a minority. The combination of cardiac and renal involvement in the same patient, particularly with nephrotic range proteinuria and a low blood pressure in someone previously normotensive, is characteristic. Diagnosis requires both identification of the clonal protein and histological confirmation with typing of the deposits, because transthyretin amyloidosis produces an almost identical cardiac picture but is treated entirely differently, and untreated light chain disease with cardiac involvement has a survival measured in months.
key_points: Wall thickening with low voltage complexes indicates infiltration, not hypertrophy
A previously hypertensive patient becoming normotensive is a warning sign
Macroglossia and periorbital purpura are specific but insensitive
Typing the deposits is essential because treatment differs entirely by type
Persistently elevated troponin without dynamic change reflects infiltration
explanation.pearls: Cardiac involvement is what determines survival in light chain amyloidosis, and the N terminal pro B type natriuretic peptide and troponin are used together to stage the disease and to decide whether a patient can tolerate the chemotherapy directed at the underlying plasma cell clone.

sources.label: HSANZ: Systemic amyloidosis diagnosis and management

subtopic_detail: A persistent platelet count of 780 with a normal C reactive protein and ferritin in a sixty two year old who has had a transient ischaemic attack
stem:
You are the physician reviewing a 62 year old woman six weeks after an episode of right arm weakness and slurred speech that resolved completely within an hour. Carotid imaging, echocardiography and prolonged rhythm monitoring during that admission were all normal.

Her platelet count was 762 x10^9/L at the time and has been between 740 and 790 on four counts over the eight months before the event. She has no bleeding, no recent surgery and no inflammatory symptoms. On examination the splenic edge is palpable 2 cm below the costal margin. Her C reactive protein and ferritin are both normal, a blood film shows large platelets with occasional giant forms, and JAK2 V617F testing is positive.

data_table.Examination: No residual neurological deficit, splenic edge palpable 2 cm below the left costal margin, no lymphadenopathy, no bruising or petechiae, no livedo or digital ischaemia
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 780 x10^9/L (150 to 400), haemoglobin 134 g/L (115 to 155), white cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein within normal limits, ferritin 92 micrograms/L (30 to 200), blood film shows large platelets with occasional giant forms, JAK2 V617F positive, BCR-ABL1 not detected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start low dose aspirin alone and repeat the blood count in six months
options.rationale: Antiplatelet therapy alone is appropriate for patients at low or intermediate risk, but it does not reduce the platelet count and is insufficient where both age over 60 and a prior thrombotic event are present. Leaving the count unchecked in a high risk patient accepts a recurrence rate that treatment can lower. (Source: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management)
source_refs: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management

options.text: Start aspirin and refer for cytoreductive therapy with hydroxycarbamide
options.rationale: Age over 60 and a previous arterial thrombotic event each place her in the high risk group, and the combination of antiplatelet therapy with cytoreduction to bring the platelet count into the normal range is what reduces recurrent thrombosis in that group. Hydroxycarbamide is the usual first line cytoreductive agent, with interferon preferred in younger patients and in pregnancy. (Source: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management)
source_refs: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management

options.text: Start oral iron replacement and repeat the blood count in three months
options.rationale: Iron deficiency is a common cause of reactive thrombocytosis, but her ferritin is normal, so there is no deficiency to replace. The near pair here is that a raised platelet count with a low ferritin would make iron replacement the correct first move, with the count expected to normalise as iron is restored. (Source: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management)
source_refs: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management

options.text: Start therapeutic anticoagulation and repeat the blood count in six months
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is directed at venous thrombosis and at cardioembolic stroke, and her extensive cardiac and rhythm investigation was negative while her event was arterial. Antiplatelet therapy rather than anticoagulation is the appropriate antithrombotic in this setting. (Source: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management)
source_refs: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management

options.text: Repeat the blood count in three months before any treatment is started
options.rationale: Persistence has already been established over eight months and four counts, and the clonal marker is positive, so further observation adds nothing. Delay in a patient who has already had a cerebral event leaves her exposed to a second one. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Essential thrombocythaemia)

explanation.summary: A persistently raised platelet count is far more often reactive than clonal, with iron deficiency, infection, inflammation, malignancy, recent surgery and hyposplenism accounting for the great majority, so a normal C reactive protein and ferritin in a patient with no inflammatory illness is what shifts the probability towards a myeloproliferative neoplasm. Supporting features include splenomegaly, large and giant platelets on the film, and a driver mutation, with JAK2 V617F present in around 60 per cent and CALR or MPL mutations in most of the remainder, while the absence of BCR-ABL1 excludes chronic myeloid leukaemia presenting with thrombocytosis. Risk stratification in essential thrombocythaemia is based on age over 60, a previous thrombotic event, and the presence of the JAK2 mutation, and it determines treatment rather than the platelet count itself. Paradoxically, counts above about 1500 x10^9/L increase bleeding risk through an acquired von Willebrand syndrome, so aspirin is used cautiously at extreme counts.
key_points: Reactive causes account for most raised platelet counts and are excluded first
Normal inflammatory markers and ferritin shift probability towards clonal disease
Risk stratification uses age, prior thrombosis and mutation status
High risk disease is treated with antiplatelet therapy plus cytoreduction
Very high counts increase bleeding risk through acquired von Willebrand syndrome
explanation.pearls: A platelet count above about 1500 x10^9/L can cause an acquired von Willebrand syndrome by adsorbing high molecular weight multimers onto the platelet surface, so a patient presenting with mucosal bleeding rather than thrombosis needs von Willebrand testing before aspirin is started.

sources.label: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management

subtopic_detail: An ulcer with a violaceous undermined border that doubled in size after debridement in a woman with ulcerative colitis and sterile wound cultures
stem:
You are the physician asked to review a 44 year old woman with ulcerative colitis who has a painful ulcer on her left shin. It began as a tender red lump at the site of a cannula three weeks ago and has enlarged rapidly since.

She has completed two courses of oral antibiotics without benefit. She underwent surgical debridement eight days ago and the ulcer has doubled in size since, now extending well beyond the debrided margin. She has no fever and no systemic upset, and she describes the pain as far worse than the appearance suggests. The ulcer has a violaceous undermined edge with a boggy necrotic base, deep wound swabs and tissue cultures have grown no organisms, and a biopsy from the ulcer edge reports a dense neutrophilic infiltrate with no organisms on special stains and no vasculitis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: An 8 cm ulcer on the left shin with a violaceous undermined border and a boggy necrotic base, marked tenderness disproportionate to the appearance, surrounding skin without spreading erythema or crepitus, pedal pulses present, no lymphangitis
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 11.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 46 mg/L (less than 5), lactate 1.1 mmol/L (less than 2.0), deep wound swab and tissue culture no growth, ankle brachial index 1.0 bilaterally, biopsy from the ulcer edge shows a dense neutrophilic infiltrate with no organisms on special stains and no vasculitis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange urgent surgical debridement and start intravenous antibiotics
options.rationale: She has already deteriorated after one debridement, which is the characteristic response of this condition to surgical trauma, and she has no fever, a normal lactate and sterile cultures. Repeating the operation would enlarge the ulcer further. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Start intravenous vancomycin and review the wound again in 48 hours
options.rationale: Two courses of antibiotics have already failed and repeated deep cultures are sterile, so a third antimicrobial addresses an infection that the evidence does not support. Continuing down the infective pathway delays the immunosuppression that would halt the ulcer. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Start systemic corticosteroid and avoid further surgical debridement
options.rationale: A rapidly enlarging ulcer with a violaceous undermined border, pain out of proportion, onset at a site of minor trauma, sterile cultures, a sterile neutrophilic infiltrate on biopsy and marked worsening after debridement describes pyoderma gangrenosum with pathergy, for which systemic immunosuppression is the treatment and further surgery is actively harmful. High dose corticosteroid or ciclosporin is used first line, with treatment of the associated bowel disease in parallel. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Apply negative pressure wound therapy and review the wound in 48 hours
options.rationale: Negative pressure therapy applies mechanical stress to the wound edge and can provoke the same pathergic enlargement as debridement in an untreated lesion. It has a role only once the inflammation has been suppressed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Take a further wound swab and review once the culture is reported
options.rationale: Deep tissue culture has already been obtained and is sterile, and a superficial swab adds nothing beyond surface colonisation. The near pair here is that tissue rather than surface sampling is what excludes infection, and that has already been done. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Pyoderma gangrenosum)

explanation.summary: Pyoderma gangrenosum is a neutrophilic dermatosis that is frequently mistaken for a necrotising soft tissue infection, and the consequences of that error are severe because surgery makes it worse through pathergy, the tendency of the lesion to extend in response to trauma. About half of cases are associated with an underlying systemic disease, most often inflammatory bowel disease, inflammatory arthritis or a haematological disorder, so a new rapidly enlarging ulcer in a patient with ulcerative colitis should raise it immediately. The clinical signature is a rapidly expanding ulcer with a violaceous undermined border, pain out of proportion to the appearance, onset at a site of minor trauma such as a cannula or a surgical incision, and failure to respond to antibiotics with sterile cultures. There is no confirmatory test, so it remains a diagnosis of exclusion supported by a biopsy showing sterile neutrophilic inflammation, and biopsy should be taken from the edge while accepting that the biopsy site itself may ulcerate.
key_points: Pathergy means surgical trauma enlarges the lesion rather than controlling it
Pain disproportionate to the appearance is characteristic
Sterile deep tissue cultures and failed antibiotics argue against infection
Around half of cases have an associated systemic disease
Diagnosis is one of exclusion supported by sterile neutrophilic histology
explanation.pearls: Necrotising fasciitis is the diagnosis that must not be missed while making this one, and the discriminators are systemic toxicity with a raised lactate, rapidly spreading erythema and crepitus, none of which is present in an afebrile patient with a normal lactate and a well demarcated violaceous border.

sources.label: GESA: Inflammatory bowel disease clinical update

subtopic_detail: Painless burns on the fingers with loss of pain and temperature over both shoulders and preserved vibration sense in a thirty two year old
stem:
You are the neurologist seeing a 32 year old chef referred because he keeps burning his fingers on pans without noticing until he sees the blister. He has also dropped several plates over the past year and says his hands feel clumsy.

He mentions a dull ache at the back of his head that comes on when he coughs or strains and lasts a few seconds. He had a whiplash injury in a car accident eight years ago. On examination he cannot feel pinprick or the cold of a tuning fork across both shoulders, the upper chest and the outer arms, while light touch, vibration and joint position sense are entirely normal in the same distribution. There is wasting of both hands with absent biceps and supinator reflexes, and the knee and ankle reflexes are brisk.

data_table.Examination: Loss of pinprick and temperature sensation over both shoulders, upper chest and outer arms with preserved light touch, vibration and joint position sense in the same distribution, wasting of the small muscles of both hands, absent biceps and supinator reflexes, brisk knee and ankle reflexes with equivocal plantar responses, healed painless burns on several fingers, no papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, vitamin B12 and folate within normal limits, serum copper within normal limits, glycated haemoglobin within normal limits, syphilis serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies and review once they are reported
options.rationale: Nerve conduction studies assess peripheral nerve, and a peripheral neuropathy does not produce sensory loss confined to one modality in a cape distribution with brisk reflexes in the legs. The pattern here localises to the spinal cord rather than to peripheral nerve. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the cervical spine, then reassess him
options.rationale: Computed tomography images bone well but resolves the spinal cord itself poorly and can miss an intramedullary fluid cavity entirely. The near pair here is trauma, where computed tomography is the correct first study because the question is bony injury. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Measure vitamin B12 and copper, then review once the results return
options.rationale: Both deficiencies cause a myelopathy but affect the dorsal columns, producing loss of vibration and joint position sense with preserved pain and temperature, which is the opposite of this pattern. Both have in any case already been measured and are normal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer for carpal tunnel decompression and review him postoperatively
options.rationale: Median nerve compression causes sensory loss in the radial three and a half digits with thenar wasting, not a bilateral cape distribution across the shoulders, and it does not abolish the biceps reflex or produce brisk leg reflexes. Operating would leave the cord lesion untreated. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Syringomyelia)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the spine and craniocervical junction
options.rationale: Loss of pain and temperature with preserved dorsal column sensation in a cape distribution reflects interruption of fibres crossing in the central cord, and the combination with lower motor neuron signs in the arms and upper motor neuron signs in the legs localises to an expanding central cervical cord lesion. Imaging must include the craniocervical junction because a hindbrain malformation is the commonest underlying cause and determines the operation performed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Dissociated sensory loss, meaning impairment of pain and temperature with preservation of light touch, vibration and joint position sense, is one of the most localising findings in clinical neurology, because it reflects damage to the spinothalamic fibres as they decussate in the central cord while the dorsal columns run uncrossed and are spared. A fluid filled cavity expanding within the central cervical cord produces this in a cape distribution across the shoulders and arms, together with wasting and loss of reflexes at the level of the lesion from anterior horn cell involvement, and brisk reflexes below it from corticospinal tract compression. Painless burns and unnoticed injuries are a characteristic presenting complaint and may precede weakness by years. Most cases are associated with a Chiari type 1 malformation, in which cerebellar tonsillar descent obstructs cerebrospinal fluid flow and produces the cough induced occipital headache, and the remainder follow trauma, meningitis or a cord tumour.
key_points: Dissociated sensory loss localises to the crossing fibres in the central cord
A cape distribution reflects a cervical central cord lesion
Lower motor neuron signs at the level with upper motor neuron signs below is the pattern
Cough induced occipital headache suggests a hindbrain malformation
Imaging must include the craniocervical junction, not the cervical spine alone
explanation.pearls: Because a cavity can extend far beyond the symptomatic level and a second cavity may sit elsewhere in the cord, the whole spine rather than the cervical region alone is imaged, and an unrecognised thoracic extension is a common reason for apparent failure of decompressive surgery.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation Australia: Clinical guidelines for stroke management
